articles.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist
articles.text:
U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist
- Date:
  November 22, 2026
- Source:
  Annenberg Public Policy Center of the University of Pennsylvania
- Summary:
  The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, and a new survey reveals widespread misconceptions about the deadly disease and its vaccine. With measles cases surging, more than one-third of Americans still believe or are uncertain about the debunked vaccine-autism link, while most don't know the disease's risks or how many vaccine doses children need.
- Share:
The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, marking a major setback in the fight against a highly contagious disease. At the same time, a new nationwide survey from the Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC) reveals that many Americans remain confused about the dangers of measles and the vaccines that protect against it.
The United States first achieved measles elimination status in 2000. This designation meant that no strain of the virus had spread continuously within the country for 12 months or longer. However, on Nov. 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization confirmed that the United States no longer qualified for that status.
The announcement comes during the country's worst measles resurgence in decades. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the United States had recorded 5,412 confirmed cases in 2026 as of Nov. 12. That is more than twice the 2,290 cases reported throughout all of 2025.
Vaccine Myths Persist Despite Decades of Scientific Evidence
A November 2026 Annenberg Science and Public Health (ASAPH) survey, conducted using adults from the SSRS Omnibus survey, highlights widespread misunderstandings about childhood vaccination. Nearly two-thirds of Americans (64%) correctly rejected the claim that "vaccines given to children for diseases like measles, mumps, and rubella cause autism." However, 17% believed the claim was true, while another 19% said they did not know whether it was true or false.
The results closely resemble findings from earlier APPC research. Across four surveys involving a separate sample of U.S. adults (September 2024 to August 2026), the ongoing ASAPH national probability survey found that 65% to 68% correctly rejected a connection between childhood vaccines and autism (65%-68%). Another 12% to 14% incorrectly believed there was a connection (12%-14%), while 19% to 22% remained uncertain.
The latest survey also asked respondents to compare autism rates among fully vaccinated and unvaccinated children. Nearly half (49%) believed both groups were "about as likely" to show signs of autism. Another 11% thought fully vaccinated children were "more likely" to show signs, 14% believed they were "less likely," and 26% could not say.
Extensive scientific research has found no evidence that vaccines cause autism. In 2004, the National Academy of Medicine (then named the Institute of Medicine) concluded that "the body of epidemiological evidence favors rejection of a causal relationship between the MMR vaccine and autism evidence."
The World Health Organization's Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety reached the same conclusion in 2025, reaffirming that high-quality scientific evidence does not establish a causal relationship between vaccination and autism. FactCheck.org, which is operated by the Annenberg Public Policy Center, has also challenged claims linking vaccines to autism, explaining that the evidence does not support them.
These misconceptions may have consequences for vaccination decisions. Previous Annenberg research found that people who accept false vaccine claims, including the belief that the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine causes autism, are less likely to recommend MMR vaccination to people who are eligible to receive it.
Only 9% of Americans Know How Deadly Measles Can Be
The survey uncovered another striking knowledge gap. Most Americans appear uncertain about the risk of death associated with measles in children.
When asked how many children infected with measles are likely to die from the disease, 59% of respondents said they did not know. Just 9% selected the correct response, "about 1 in 1,000," which most closely matches the CDC’s estimate that 1 to 3 of every 1,000 infected children die from respiratory or neurological complications.
Nearly one-quarter of respondents (23%) underestimated the death rate, while another 9% selected a higher rate.
Knowledge about measles vaccination was also limited. Almost half of Americans (49%) said they were unsure how many doses children need for full protection. Only about one-third (34%) correctly identified the recommended two-dose schedule.
The CDC advises giving children their first MMR vaccine dose between 12 and 15 months of age, followed by a second dose between ages 4 and 6. According to CDC data, a single dose provides 93% protection against measles, while receiving both doses increases effectiveness to 97%.
Public Confidence in Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Remains Low
The survey also examined Americans' trust in U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The findings indicate that public confidence in his health-related communications has changed little since earlier surveys conducted in 2025 and 2026.
In November 2026, about six in 10 respondents (61%) said they were not confident that Kennedy was providing trustworthy information about public health. The remaining four in 10 (39%) expressed confidence in the information he provides.
These results are consistent with seven earlier national probability surveys conducted over two years (February 2025 to August 2026). During that period, 60% to 63% of respondents reported lacking confidence in Kennedy, while 37% to 39% expressed confidence.
Kathleen Hall Jamieson, director of the Annenberg Public Policy Center's Science of Science Communication Institute and its ASAPH and ASK surveys, said the loss of measles elimination status demonstrates the consequences of declining vaccination coverage.
"The announcement that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status confirms what we already knew," said Kathleen Hall Jamieson. "Those who refused the MMR vaccine for themselves or their children and those who misled them into doing so have produced the tragic effects that science predicted would occur when community immunity dropped below the threshold needed to protect those who are not able to be vaccinated or refused to be."
How the National Measles Survey Was Conducted
The findings draw on two types of Annenberg Science and Public Health (ASAPH) surveys.
The November 2026 results come from a nationally representative survey of 1,028 U.S. adults conducted for APPC by SSRS, an independent market research organization. Participants were selected from the company's probability-based online opinion panel, and responses were collected Nov. 6-8, 2026. The survey has a margin of sampling error (MOE) of ± 3.5 percentage points at the 95% confidence level.
The other findings come from APPC's ongoing ASAPH panel surveys, which are also administered by SSRS. Participants were originally recruited through probability sampling from the SSRS Opinion Panel, and their responses are weighted to reflect the U.S. adult population. This research panel operates separately from the SSRS Omnibus survey and has completed more than 30 survey waves since April 2021.
Percentages are rounded to the nearest whole number, so totals may not always equal 100%.
Additional results are available in the survey topline, which includes data from both the November 2026 omnibus survey and the ongoing ASAPH panel surveys. A separate methodology statement provides further details about the latest survey.
Since April 2021, the Annenberg Public Policy Center has used its Annenberg Science and Public Health (ASAPH) research program and separate national samples to monitor Americans' knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors related to vaccines, Covid-19, influenza, RSV, and other important health issues.
The APPC health survey team includes Ken Winneg, managing director of survey research; Laura A. Gibson, research analyst; and Patrick E. Jamieson, director of the Annenberg Health and Risk Communication Institute.

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging
articles.text:
Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging
- Date:
  November 22, 2026
- Source:
  Radiological Society of North America
- Summary:
  Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than scientists previously realized, with new research linking lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. The surprising connection suggests that routine medical scans could help uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.
- Share:
Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than previously understood. A new study from Johns Hopkins University found that people with lower bone density in their spine experienced faster cognitive decline and more rapid deterioration of the brain's white matter as they aged.
The findings, published in Radiology, a journal of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), suggest that bone health and brain aging may be more closely connected than scientists once realized.
Bone mineral density reflects how much mineral material, including calcium, is present in a given volume of bone. Lower density makes bones more fragile and increases the likelihood of fractures. Although the effects of bone loss on skeletal health are well established, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how declining bone density might relate to changes in the brain.
Using AI to Investigate Bone Density and Brain Health
To explore this connection, a research team led by Sara Momtazmanesh, M.D., a postdoctoral research fellow in the Department of Radiology and Radiological Sciences at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, examined existing data from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). The analysis included information from participants who had undergone chest CT scans without contrast dye, multiple types of brain MRI examinations, and tests measuring cognitive performance.
The researchers applied a deep learning algorithm developed in the laboratory of Shadpour Demehri, M.D., a Johns Hopkins professor of radiology. The AI system analyzed non-contrast chest CT images from 2,086 MESA participants to determine their initial thoracic vertebral volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD), a measurement of bone density in the spine.
Of those participants, 715 had the required bone density measurements along with brain MRI results and cognitive testing, making them eligible for the final study group.
The researchers examined the MRI scans for two indicators of changes in the brain's white matter. The first was white matter hyperintensities, areas of abnormal tissue that appear unusually bright on certain MRI images. The second was reduced fractional anisotropy, a measurement that can indicate deterioration in the microscopic organization of white matter. Both types of changes have been associated with cognitive decline and a greater risk of dementia.
Follow-up imaging data were available for 408 participants for white matter hyperintensities and 405 participants for fractional anisotropy, allowing researchers to examine how these brain changes progressed over time.
Lower Bone Density Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline
The analysis revealed a notable pattern: participants with lower spinal bone density at the beginning of the study tended to experience a faster decline in overall cognitive performance.
The researchers also identified changes in specific brain regions that are important for thinking and memory. Lower bone density was associated with greater accumulation of white matter hyperintensities in the corpus callosum, a structure that supports executive function, working memory, and attention.
Another connection emerged in the anterior limb of the internal capsule, a brain region involved in executive function. Participants with lower bone density showed a more pronounced decline in fractional anisotropy in this area, suggesting worsening white matter integrity.
"This study is the first longitudinal secondary analysis linking baseline vertebral bone mineral density to changes in white matter structure, white matter hyperintensity progression and cognition," Dr. Demehri said. "This comprehensive study using both imaging and clinical assessments sends a clear signal that bone density at baseline is associated with both functional and imaging measures of age-related brain degeneration."
Does Bone Loss Cause Dementia?
Despite the connection between weaker bones and declining brain health, the researchers emphasized that their findings do not establish that osteoporosis causes dementia.
Instead, bone deterioration and brain degeneration may be consequences of some of the same biological changes that occur with aging.
"This study is not about cause and effect, but rather the observation of a metabolic syndrome that may cause both bone and brain degeneration," Dr. Demehri said. "The co-occurrence observed in the study may reflect shared metabolic drivers of aging, including insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and menopausal change, rather than a direct bone-to-brain effect."
These findings raise the possibility that identifying people with reduced bone density could also help recognize those at greater risk of neurological decline. Earlier identification might create opportunities for additional screening and better management of risk factors that affect both skeletal and brain health.
Routine CT Scans Could Reveal Hidden Signs of Brain Aging
One potentially valuable implication of the research is that doctors may be able to obtain useful information about bone density from CT scans that patients have already received for unrelated medical reasons.
"Chest CT is done for lung cancer screening, calcium scoring, nodule follow-up, and many other indications," Dr. Momtazmanesh said. "These scans could provide an opportunistic measurement of bone density from the thoracic spine that is associated with a loss of cognitive function."
By using AI to analyze existing medical images, researchers may be able to identify patterns of age-related disease that would otherwise go unnoticed. This approach could also help scientists investigate why conditions affecting different parts of the body often develop together.
Dr. Demehri concurred: "Diagnostic images contain an immense amount of data that AI can now synthesize at scale across multiple organ systems. This creates a robust, newly feasible opportunity to interconnect co-existing age-related pathologies that have traditionally been studied in isolation and to identify shared biological pathways and potential common causal mechanisms."
The study highlights a potentially important connection between bone health and cognitive function, while also demonstrating how AI could make routine medical imaging more informative. Although further research is needed to understand the biological mechanisms involved, the findings suggest that measurements taken from the spine may provide valuable clues about changes occurring in the aging brain.
The study, "Deep Learning-derived Bone Mineral Density and Longitudinal White Matter Microstructure and Cognitive Decline: Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis," also included Quincy A. Hathaway, M.D., Ph.D., Michael P. Bancks, Ph.D., M.P.H., David A. Bluemke, M.D., M.S.B., Ph.D., R. Graham Barr, M.D., Dr.P.H., Wendy S. Demehri and Momtazmanesh.

articles.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
articles.text:
Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
- Date:
  November 22, 2026
- Source:
  Estonian Research Council
- Summary:
  Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.
- Share:
Medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut. A large study from the University of Tartu Institute of Genomics has found that many commonly prescribed drugs leave lasting changes in the gut microbiome, even long after people stop using them.
The gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract. These microbes play important roles in digestion, immune function, and overall health. While antibiotics are well known for disrupting gut bacteria, the new findings suggest that many other medications can also have effects that persist for years.
To investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort. They discovered that most of the medications studied were associated with changes in gut bacteria. Even more surprisingly, a substantial number left detectable microbial "fingerprints" years after patients had stopped taking them.
Common Medications Leave Lasting Changes in Gut Bacteria
The findings extend far beyond antibiotics. Antidepressants, beta-blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and benzodiazepines were all linked to differences in the gut microbiome.
These medications are widely used to treat everyday health conditions. Beta-blockers are commonly prescribed for high blood pressure and certain heart conditions, while proton pump inhibitors reduce stomach acid and are frequently used to treat acid reflux. Benzodiazepines are often prescribed for anxiety, and antidepressants help manage depression and other mental health conditions.
"Most microbiome studies only consider current medications, but our results show that past drug use can be just as important as it is a surprisingly strong factor in explaining individual microbiome differences," said Dr. Oliver Aasmets, lead author.
This discovery suggests that looking only at the medications someone currently takes may overlook an important part of their gut health history. Previous prescriptions could help explain why the composition of gut bacteria differs so much from one person to another.
Anxiety Medications Show Effects Comparable to Antibiotics
One of the most striking findings involved benzodiazepines, a class of medications commonly used to treat anxiety.
Researchers found that these drugs were associated with changes in the gut microbiome comparable to those seen with broad-spectrum antibiotics. These antibiotics target a wide variety of bacteria and are known to substantially alter the microbial communities living in the digestive system.
The researchers also discovered that medications within the same drug class did not necessarily produce the same effects. For example, diazepam and alprazolam are both benzodiazepines used to treat similar conditions, yet they appeared to differ in how strongly they disrupted gut bacteria.
This suggests that the effects of medication on the microbiome may depend not only on the type of drug being taken, but also on the specific medication.
Gut Bacteria Can Change When Medications Are Started or Stopped
To investigate whether medications were actually contributing to these microbial changes, researchers collected additional stool samples from a smaller group of participants.
By examining how the microbiome changed when people started or stopped certain medications, the team identified predictable shifts in gut bacteria. These findings provided additional evidence that the drugs themselves were contributing to the changes, rather than simply being associated with differences already present in patients.
Although the number of participants in this follow-up analysis was relatively small, the researchers were able to verify lasting effects associated with several drug categories. These included proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and certain antibiotics, including combinations of penicillins and macrolides.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, often called SSRIs, are a widely prescribed type of antidepressant. Macrolides are a class of antibiotics used to treat various bacterial infections.
Why Your Medication History May Matter More Than Previously Thought
The findings point to an important consideration for researchers studying the relationship between gut bacteria and disease. Differences in the microbiome may reflect not only a person's current health and medication use, but also treatments received years earlier.
If previous medications are not taken into account, scientists could mistakenly attribute certain microbial differences to a disease or another health factor when past drug exposure may have contributed.
The results also highlight how much remains to be understood about the long-term relationship between medications and the gut microbiome. Although the study identified persistent microbial changes, these findings do not establish that such changes are necessarily harmful or that they lead to specific health problems.
"This is a comprehensive systematic evaluation of long-term medication effects on the microbiome using real-world medical health records," said Professor Elin Org, corresponding author. "We hope this encourages researchers and clinicians to factor in medication history when interpreting microbiome data."

articles.title: Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds
articles.text:
Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds
- Date:
  November 22, 2026
- Source:
  Curtin University
- Summary:
  People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major new review of 40 studies. Researchers estimate that nearly five out of every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimer’s each year. By focusing specifically on these two conditions, the study offers a clearer understanding of a potentially serious connection between metabolic health and brain health.
- Share:
A major research review led by Curtin University has found that people with type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. The findings provide a clearer picture of the connection between diabetes and Alzheimer's, including how much the risk increases and how frequently new cases occur.
Researchers analyzed data from 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis. They estimated that for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes, approximately 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease over the course of one year.
A separate analysis found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53 percent higher adjusted relative risk of developing Alzheimer's compared with those without the condition.
Understanding the Link Between Diabetes and Alzheimer's
Study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, an NHMRC Investigator Fellow at the Curtin School of Population Health, explained that the findings offer a more precise understanding of Alzheimer's risk among people with type 2 diabetes.
Unlike previous research reviews that often examined multiple forms of diabetes or dementia together, this analysis concentrated specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease. It also measured how frequently people with diabetes developed Alzheimer's, providing an additional perspective on the connection between the two conditions.
"While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often new cases occurred," Dr. Adewuyi said.
"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes."
The study, "Incidence and risk of Alzheimer's disease in individuals with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis," was published in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy.

articles.title: Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed
articles.text:
Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed
- Date:
  November 22, 2026
- Source:
  Universe Today
- Summary:
  Scientists have discovered a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel: at extreme speeds, the light propelling futuristic solar sails could actually begin slowing them down. Once a spacecraft reaches 75% of the speed of light, some scattered light starts producing drag, potentially complicating humanity’s plans to reach distant stars.
- Share:
Reaching another star will require spacecraft capable of traveling far faster than anything humanity has built so far. Conventional rockets powered by chemical fuel simply cannot achieve the enormous speeds needed to cross the distances between stars within a practical amount of time. One promising alternative is the solar sail, a vast, lightweight reflective surface that uses the momentum of light to propel a spacecraft through space.
Some proposed interstellar missions would take this concept even further by using powerful lasers to push sails to extraordinary speeds, potentially reaching a substantial fraction of the speed of light. However, new research suggests that this approach comes with an unexpected complication. At extreme speeds, some of the very light driving the spacecraft forward could begin acting against it.
In a recent paper available on arXiv, Chao Shen and Jiaze Li of the Harbin Institute of Technology investigate how light interacts with a rapidly accelerating solar sail. Their findings reveal a surprising source of resistance that emerges as the spacecraft approaches 75% of the speed of light.
How Light Can Push a Spacecraft Through Space
Although light has no mass, it carries momentum and can transfer that momentum to objects it strikes. This creates a tiny pushing force known as radiation pressure. Under ordinary conditions, the effect is extremely weak, but in the vacuum of space, a large reflective sail can gradually build up speed as light continues to strike its surface.
For spacecraft traveling between stars, powerful lasers could provide a much more concentrated source of light than the Sun. By directing an intense beam at a sail, engineers hope to accelerate extremely small probes to speeds that conventional propulsion systems cannot approach.
The researchers examined three ways that photons, the individual packets of energy that make up light, transfer momentum to a sail. These interactions are incident light (that raw momentum of the photons hitting the sail), specular reflection (momentum imparted when photons bounce perfectly off the sail), and diffuse scattering (momentum from photons that are absorbed by the sail then reemitted in random directions).
According to the study, these three contributions affect the sail's motion with different levels of efficiency. Incident light provides the strongest contribution in the researchers' breakdown, followed by specular reflection and then diffuse scattering.
A Strange Problem Emerges Near the Speed of Light
The situation becomes considerably more complicated once a solar sail reaches relativistic speeds, meaning speeds high enough that the effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become important.
As the sail accelerates away from its laser source, it experiences an increasingly strong Doppler effect. This is the same basic phenomenon that changes the apparent pitch of a passing ambulance siren, except that light experiences a change in frequency rather than sound.
For the accelerating sail, the incoming laser light becomes progressively redshifted, meaning its frequency decreases from the sail's perspective. As a result, the light transfers momentum less effectively, reducing the thrust generated by all three contributions examined in the study.
In other words, the faster the spacecraft travels, the less effective its laser propulsion becomes. Even with a powerful beam continuously striking the sail, gaining additional speed becomes increasingly difficult.
Various concepts for interstellar exploration have been proposed over the years, including Breakthrough Starshot, which envisioned using powerful lasers to accelerate tiny spacecraft toward nearby stars. The new findings highlight another challenge that such ambitious missions would need to consider.
At 75% of Light Speed, Light Starts Working Against the Sail
The researchers identified an especially unusual effect once the sail reaches approximately 75% of the speed of light.
At this point, a phenomenon known as relativistic light aberration changes how the scattered light is distributed. Relativistic aberration describes how the apparent directions in which light travels are altered by motion at speeds approaching the speed of light.
From the viewpoint of an observer at rest on Earth, the diffusely scattered light becomes increasingly concentrated in the spacecraft's forward direction. Because emitting light carries momentum, the sail experiences a corresponding recoil in the opposite direction.
This means that diffuse scattering (admittedly the weakest of the three forces) begins producing drag rather than helping propel the spacecraft forward.
The result is a striking paradox: some of the light intended to accelerate an interstellar spacecraft actually begins resisting its motion.
Importantly, this does not mean the spacecraft suddenly stops accelerating or that its entire propulsion system begins pushing backward. The laser still generates a positive overall force, allowing the sail to continue gaining speed. However, the additional resistance reduces the efficiency of the system, making further acceleration more challenging.
Advanced Materials Could Help Overcome the Challenge
The study focuses specifically on the forces produced by light and does not attempt to model every obstacle a spacecraft would encounter during an interstellar journey.
For example, the researchers do not include resistance from interstellar gas and dust, which could become important at extreme velocities. They also leave out the thermal challenges associated with directing extremely powerful lasers at a thin sail. If the material absorbs too much energy, intense heating could damage or even melt it.
Another important simplification is that the calculations treat the sail as an idealized mirror. Real spacecraft would need materials capable of reflecting laser light efficiently while remaining lightweight, durable, and stable under extreme conditions.
Engineers are already exploring advanced metamaterials and photonic crystals that could help address these demands. These specially engineered materials can be designed to interact with particular wavelengths of light in ways that ordinary reflective surfaces cannot.
Intriguingly, such materials might even turn some of the relativistic effects identified in the research into an advantage. By carefully controlling how light scatters from the sail, future designs could potentially generate forces that automatically correct its orientation and position, helping it remain aligned with the laser beam throughout acceleration.
The Long Road to Interstellar Travel
Despite the promise of laser propulsion, humanity remains far from building and testing a complete solar sail system capable of reaching another star.
The physics becomes increasingly complicated over such enormous distances and at such extraordinary speeds. Additional effects, including the curvature of spacetime, would also need to be considered in a more complete description of an interstellar journey. These effects were simplified out of the new analysis.
Nevertheless, understanding how light behaves when it interacts with a spacecraft traveling at a significant fraction of light speed is an important part of making interstellar exploration possible.
If humanity eventually sends robotic probes to another star, success will depend on solving countless engineering and physics challenges. Knowing that light itself can become an unexpected source of resistance gives researchers one more piece of the puzzle, and potentially a better understanding of how to design spacecraft capable of making the journey.

articles.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
articles.text:
A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
- Date:
  November 22, 2026
- Source:
  California Institute of Technology
- Summary:
  Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.
- Share:
The biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.
New research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.
The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.
A Hidden Population of Black Holes
"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," says LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract."
Chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.
Despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.
A Mysterious Gap in Black Hole Masses
To investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.
Even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising new questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.
"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred says. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes."
The researchers also examined how quickly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).
Taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.
Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths
Finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.
"We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred says. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting."
By studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The new findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.
The research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

articles.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
articles.text:
DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
- Date:
  November 22, 2026
- Source:
  Texas A&M University
- Summary:
  Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.
- Share:
How did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions? Scientists have spent decades trying to answer this fundamental question, including how the earliest biological systems endured an environment that would have been dangerous to many living organisms today.
Researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA. Their findings could help explain how early genetic material survived intense ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.
The research was led by Dr. Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), provides new insight into a longstanding mystery surrounding molecular evolution and the origins of life.
Why DNA's Evolution Has Puzzled Scientists
One of the major changes in the evolution of genetic systems involved the transition from RNA, which is typically a single-stranded molecule, to DNA as the primary means of storing genetic information. An important difference between the two molecules is that DNA uses a chemical building block called thymine in place of uracil, which is found in RNA.
This substitution has puzzled researchers for decades. Thymine is more susceptible to certain forms of ultraviolet (UV) damage, making its adoption seem like an evolutionary disadvantage. The problem would have been especially significant on early Earth, before a protective ozone layer developed and shielded the planet's surface from much of the Sun's harmful radiation.
Why would evolution favor a component that appeared to make genetic material more vulnerable under such harsh conditions? Rentzepis and his colleagues set out to investigate whether thymine might offer an advantage that had previously been overlooked.
To explore this possibility, the researchers exposed thymine and uracil to carefully controlled UV radiation intended to reproduce conditions on primordial Earth. They analyzed the molecules using biophotonics, a field that examines biological materials through their interactions with light. Their experiments employed several techniques, including absorption, fluorescence, and Raman spectroscopy.
DNA's Surprising Defense Against UV Damage
The results revealed an unexpected possibility. Although thymine can be vulnerable to UV radiation, it appears to favor types of molecular damage that are more readily reversed. This suggests that an important advantage of thymine may lie not in preventing damage, but in limiting its consequences and making recovery easier.
"We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form, suggesting that early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight not by avoiding damage, but by controlling it and making it easier to self-repair," said Khosh Abady. "In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule."
This finding offers a possible explanation for why thymine became a fundamental component of DNA despite its apparent weakness. By concentrating UV damage in parts of the molecule where it could be more easily reversed, thymine may have helped protect the integrity of early genetic systems.
The discovery also suggests that surviving the extreme conditions of early Earth may have depended on more than simply resisting environmental threats. The ability to manage and recover from damage could have played an important role in the evolution of the molecular systems that eventually supported life.
New Possibilities for Pathogen Detection and UV Disinfection
Beyond its implications for understanding life's beginnings, the research could have practical applications in several scientific and technological fields.
The team established a new set of reference measurements describing how these molecules respond to light. These measurements could eventually help researchers identify harmful microorganisms more efficiently and assess the effectiveness of systems that use UV radiation to disinfect water and other materials.
"The distinct spectral signatures we measured could support applications in faster, more sensitive pathogen detection and in monitoring whether UV disinfection has effectively inactivated microorganisms, particularly in water-treatment systems," said Khosh Abady.
These potential applications demonstrate how investigating fundamental questions about molecular evolution can also provide tools for addressing modern challenges in health and environmental safety.
Could the Building Blocks of Life Have Come From Space?
With these findings in hand, Rentzepis and his team plan to investigate an even earlier chapter in life's history. Their next goal is to understand the forces and chemical processes that brought thymine, uracil, and other essential components of primitive genetic systems together.
A central question is whether these ingredients originated entirely on Earth or whether some arrived from beyond our planet. Meteorites may have delivered organic compounds that later became incorporated into the chemical systems from which life developed.
"We hope to explore whether life's chemical building blocks formed and assembled entirely on Earth or whether some were delivered to our planet from elsewhere by meteorites and later incorporated into early genetic systems," said Khosh Abady. "We are grateful to Texas A&M University and our research sponsors for supporting this work and enabling us to explore fundamental questions about life's origins."
By examining how DNA's molecular components respond to radiation and how those components may have first assembled, the researchers hope to uncover more of the chemical history that made life on Earth possible.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Texas A&M University. Original written by Amy Leifeste. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Keyvan Khosh Abady, Negar Karpourazar, Peter M. Rentzepis. UV photodamage pathways and the evolutionary selection of thymine over uracil in early genetic systems. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2026; 123 (33) DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2615278123

articles.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
articles.text:
A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
- Date:
  November 22, 2026
- Source:
  University of Cambridge
- Summary:
  At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.
- Share:
At an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today. Now, scientists studying his extraordinary lifespan have uncovered genetic clues that may explain how he has remained so resilient for nearly two centuries.
The findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes. His body also appears to have avoided some of the genetic changes that normally accumulate with age, helping preserve important biological functions.
In a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging. These variants influence several essential processes, including repairing damaged DNA, limiting inflammation, controlling insulin activity, and suppressing cancer.
Jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea) believed to have hatched in 1832. That means he was already alive during the lifetimes of Charles Darwin and Queen Victoria. Today, he holds the distinction of being both the oldest living giant tortoise and the oldest known living land animal.
A 194-Year-Old Tortoise With Remarkably Youthful Gene Regulation
One of the most surprising discoveries came when scientists examined Jonathan's epigenome, the system of chemical markers that helps determine which genes are switched on or off. These regulatory mechanisms typically change as animals grow older, potentially disrupting important cellular processes and contributing to age-related deterioration.
To investigate how Jonathan's biology has changed over time, the researchers compared his epigenome with those of younger giant tortoises belonging to the same species.
They found that the regulatory mechanisms associated with DNA repair and metabolism had remained remarkably stable. Despite Jonathan's advanced age, these genetic controls closely resembled those found in his much younger relatives.
The results suggest that maintaining stable gene regulation could be one of the factors helping giant tortoises withstand the biological stresses of aging for exceptionally long periods.
This research also represents the first investigation of the epigenome of a giant tortoise. The project was led by Kallel, a US nonprofit organization focused on longevity research. Its scientists believe that examining the biology of animals capable of surviving for centuries could reveal important new insights into the mechanisms of extreme longevity.
"We found that the gene regulators involved in energy production and DNA repair have remained incredibly stable in Jonathan over almost two centuries," said Dr. Justin Gerlach at Peterhouse at the University of Cambridge, who was involved in the study.
He added: "There are few creatures that could tell us more about aging than the giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands. Working with a really old giant tortoise is such a privilege: you get a sense of the tortoise being your collaborator, not your study subject."
Gerlach has spent several decades investigating giant tortoise ecology and conservation. However, this project marks his first examination of the biological mechanisms responsible for their exceptional lifespans.
Could Giant Tortoise DNA Reveal Secrets to Human Longevity?
The researchers hope Jonathan's genetic characteristics could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to slowing age-related decline and preventing chronic diseases in humans.
By identifying the biological systems that allow certain animals to remain healthy for extraordinarily long periods, researchers may be able to uncover protective mechanisms that could inform future medical treatments.
"Nature has already solved the puzzle of aging in remarkable ways, and Jonathan's genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience," said Stephen Clark, MD, PhD, founder of Kallel and senior author of the study.
He added: "Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people. Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face, and through the generosity of philanthropic partners, we can democratize access to longevity medicine."
Although the findings provide intriguing clues about extreme longevity, translating these discoveries into treatments for humans will require further research.
Nearly Two Centuries of Life on a Remote Atlantic Island
Jonathan has spent most of his exceptionally long life on St. Helena, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean. He lives on the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the island's governor.
He arrived on St. Helena from the Seychelles 144 years ago as a gift to the governor. Jonathan was already fully grown when he reached the island, providing further evidence of his remarkable age.
The giant tortoises native to the Galapagos and Seychelles islands are among the last surviving representatives of a group of enormous reptiles that once played dominant ecological roles across many of the world's islands.
Today, these extraordinary survivors offer scientists a rare opportunity to investigate how evolution has equipped certain animals to withstand the effects of time. Jonathan's unusually stable genetic regulation provides a particularly intriguing window into the biology of aging and the possibility of extending healthy life.

Materials provided by University of Cambridge. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:

Taylor, Mathia Colwell, Jonathan Hollins, Sam Pascucci, Konstantin Weissenow, Burkhard Rost, Pascal Notin, Justin Gerlach, Thomas C. Terwilliger, Li-Wei Hung, Lars Juhl Jensen, Kathlyn Reed, Todd R. Robeck, Steve Horvath, Christopher Faulk, Yanjun Ma, Stephen W. Clark. Epigenetic insights into extreme longevity in the world’s oldest terrestrial animal, Jonathan. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (41) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adw8887

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision
articles.text:
Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision
- Date:
  November 22, 2026
- Source:
  University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine
- Summary:
  Scientists have discovered a new genetic eye disease that can silently damage peripheral and night vision while leaving central sight largely unaffected for years. The condition may be detectable through an unusual difficulty adjusting to darkness, offering a potential early warning sign before irreversible retinal damage occurs.
- Share:
A newly identified genetic eye disease can gradually interfere with night vision and the ability to see objects at the edges of the visual field. The condition may be especially difficult to recognize because people can maintain good eyesight for much of their lives before noticeable problems develop.
An international research team, including scientists at the Scheie Eye Institute within the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, traced the condition to a gene already associated with another form of vision loss. However, the two diseases affect eyesight in strikingly different ways. The previously known disorder primarily damages central vision, while the newly discovered condition affects peripheral vision and the ability to see in darkness.
Although the condition has not yet received an official name, researchers are calling it EFEMP1-associated late-onset retinal degeneration (L-ORD). It is linked to a specific genetic variant known as p.Arg140Trp in the EFEMP1 gene. This change causes an unusually thick accumulation of material between cells in the eye.
A Genetic Discovery That Began Decades Ago
The investigation traces back to 1998, when doctors documented an unusual pattern of vision loss in a family in the United States. As researchers uncovered new genetic evidence, they were able to connect those findings to families in Europe who showed similar symptoms.
The study, published in JAMA Ophthalmology, examined three unrelated families from different countries who carried the p.Arg140Trp variant. Their symptoms were compared with those of another family carrying a different change in the same gene, called p.Arg345Trp, which is associated with the previously recognized disease affecting central vision.
The international collaboration included researchers from Penn Medicine, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Basel, Charles University, and the University of Bonn.
At first, scientists suspected that the unusual symptoms in the original family might be caused by a different genetic disorder. Testing, however, failed to identify the variants responsible for that condition.
"The different disease expression in this family was thought to be similar to a condition caused by C1QTNF5 gene variants. However, none of the variants associated with that disease were found," said Artur V. Cideciyan, PhD, an ophthalmology researcher and co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Our collaborators then discovered a new variant in the EFEMP1 gene that normally causes a different disease where the macula, which is tied to central vision, is affected first."
How the New Eye Disease Affects Night Vision
The researchers found that the newly identified condition develops gradually in the outer regions of the retina. Located at the back of the eye, the retina detects incoming light and transforms it into signals that the brain uses to create visual images.
Unlike the previously known EFEMP1 disorder, which initially affects the macula and central vision, this newly identified disease begins in the peripheral retina. People may see normally for much of their lives before gradually noticing that their side vision is narrowing or that seeing in dim surroundings has become more difficult.
Problems may be particularly noticeable around dusk or at night, when the eyes must rely more heavily on specialized light-sensitive cells called rods.
One reason the disease is challenging to diagnose is that these cells may initially show no visible structural damage. The gradual progression of symptoms can make the condition even harder to recognize.
However, the researchers identified a potentially valuable early clue. In affected individuals, rod cells take unusually long to recover when the eyes move from bright surroundings into darkness. This abnormal response can be detected even when the retina still appears structurally normal.
"We can detect a major abnormality in the way rod photoreceptors recover in darkness with retinas that still look structurally intact," Cideciyan said. "This gives us a functional marker of disease at a stage when photoreceptor cells have not yet been lost."
The finding suggests that changes in how the retina functions may reveal the disease before the light-sensitive cells responsible for vision begin to disappear.
What the Discovery Could Mean for Age-Related Vision Loss
An important question remains unanswered: How many people carry this newly identified genetic variant?
Researchers suspect the condition is relatively uncommon, but they do not yet have enough information to determine its prevalence. Larger investigations will be necessary to establish how frequently the variant occurs and how many people may be affected.
Beyond identifying another inherited eye disorder, the findings could help scientists better understand why vision deteriorates with age. Studying rare genetic diseases can reveal biological processes that may also contribute to much more widespread retinal conditions.
"Aging is a risk factor for many medical conditions, including retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration, the most common retinal condition of aging," said Tomas S. Aleman, MD, a professor of ophthalmology and the other co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Lessons learned from these infrequent, late-onset genetic eye diseases offer glimpses at possible mechanisms of disease for much more frequent retinal problems."
By revealing how different changes in a single gene can produce distinct patterns of vision loss, the research adds to scientists' understanding of inherited retinal disease. It also highlights the potential importance of detecting changes in visual function before damage becomes apparent in the retina's structure.
The study received support from the University of Edinburgh Chancellor's Fellowship award, RS Macdonald Charitable Trust Seedcorn Award, the BrightFocus Foundation (M2024009N), the German Research Foundation (532367710), the Medical Research Council (MC_UU_00035/9, MC_UU_00007/10), the Swiss National Science Foundation (204285), the Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic (NW24-06-00083), Charles University in Prague (UNCE/24/MED/022 and SVV 2600631), and the Samuel G. Jacobson, MD, PhD, Memorial Fund.

Journal Reference:
- Chloe M. Stanton, Georg Ansari, Kristina Pfau, Theresa Lipsky, Mihail Halachev, Lukas Gerasimavicius, Camilla Drake, Joseph A. Marsh, Caroline Hayward, Alexander Sumaroka, Bohdan Kousal, Petra Lišková, Mathieu Quinodoz, Carlo Rivolta, Tomas S. Aleman, Artur V. Cideciyan, Maximilian Pfau. Widening the Spectrum of Disease Expression due to Heterozygous Variants in EFEMP1. JAMA Ophthalmology, 2026; 144 (10): 915 DOI: 10.1001/jamaophthalmol.2026.3828

articles.title: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
articles.text:
AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
- Date:
  November 21, 2026
- Source:
  University of Plymouth
- Summary:
  Scientists have developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a major study involving nearly 70,000 patients. By revealing subtle patterns that conventional screening misses, the technology could help doctors detect cancer earlier and spare patients unnecessary invasive procedures.
- Share:
Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult. Its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions, including kidney stones, allowing warning signs to go unnoticed.
Researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis. In some patients, the technology detected subtle warning signals dating back as far as five years.
The new approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked. By recognizing these patterns, researchers hope to make bladder cancer screening more accurate and help doctors find the disease when treatment is most likely to succeed.
AI Finds Hidden Bladder Cancer Clues in Medical Records
Under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs of bladder cancer is visible blood in the urine (hematuria). However, blood in the urine can also result from noncancerous problems, including kidney stones and prostate conditions. This overlap makes it difficult to determine which patients need further investigation and contributes to missed cases.
Confirming bladder cancer currently requires a procedure called cystoscopy (where a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder). Although effective, the examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients who are most likely to have the disease.
To explore a possible solution, a team led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients. The records covered a 25-year period, from 1995 through 2020.
The researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators (from smoking and exercise habits to medication use). From this enormous collection of information, the system narrowed the list to 38 features that were especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk.
AI Identifies 85% of Bladder Cancer Cases
The results suggest that AI could substantially improve the way patients are assessed for bladder cancer.
The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not have the disease. It also performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.
Importantly, the system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis. Some of the warning signals it recognized could be traced back up to five years, suggesting that valuable clues may exist in medical records long before cancer is discovered.
The AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors, including smoking and blood in the urine. However, it also uncovered unexpected associations that conventional screening approaches would be unlikely to detect.
For example, patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appeared to have a lower risk of bladder cancer. Meanwhile, long-term use of tamoxifen (a breast cancer medication) was associated with a higher risk.
These findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it. Instead, they raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms that researchers believe deserve closer examination.
Another surprising finding involved blood in the urine. Although this symptom is often considered a major warning sign, its significance appears to depend partly on a patient's other medical conditions. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, for instance, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk.
Understanding these relationships more fully could eventually help doctors distinguish patients who need urgent investigation from those who may not require invasive testing.
A New Approach to Early Cancer Screening
Beyond identifying warning signs, the AI system could also divide patients into three groups according to their estimated likelihood of having bladder cancer: low-risk (below 7% probability), uncertain (grey zone: 7-55%), and high-risk (above 55%).
This approach could help healthcare providers decide which patients need immediate attention and which may benefit from additional monitoring.
For example, patients in the uncertain category might be monitored before undergoing procedures such as cystoscopy. If further research confirms the system's reliability, this could reduce unnecessary examinations while allowing doctors to concentrate resources on people at greatest risk.
PhD student Xu Wang, who led the data analysis, said: "Bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022."
"Despite its prevalence, no routine screening program exists for the general population, and - following symptoms - detection relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Our system goes far beyond traditional symptoms, and it's great to have uncovered the results that we have. The research shows that the combination of multiple factors - from medication histories to seemingly unrelated conditions - can reveal patterns invisible to conventional screening methods."
Could AI Help Doctors Catch Bladder Cancer Earlier?
The potential benefits extend beyond improving diagnostic accuracy. Detecting bladder cancer earlier could mean more treatment options, better survival outcomes, and fewer patients undergoing invasive procedures unnecessarily.
Dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, emphasized the importance of developing better screening methods.
"Bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families.
"It could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier, when survival outcomes and quality of life can be dramatically improved."
Professor Shang-Ming Zhou believes the findings point toward a more individualized approach to cancer screening, in which AI helps doctors interpret a patient's broader medical history rather than relying primarily on individual symptoms.
"This work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.
"By harnessing the power of interpretable machine learning and comprehensive health records, we're moving closer to detecting this disease at its earliest, most treatable stages."
More Research Needed Before Clinical Use
Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use.
All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Before the model can be introduced into other healthcare settings, researchers will need to determine whether it performs equally well with different patient populations and medical record systems.
Professor Zhou explained why broader testing is essential.
"It's important to emphasize that further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely - for example, all of the data analyzed came from the SAIL database in Wales, so we'd want to investigate other datasets too.
"But it's a very exciting early study. Additional studies would also be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions."
The findings offer an encouraging glimpse of how artificial intelligence might improve cancer screening by uncovering patterns hidden within years of routine medical information. With further validation, such tools could help doctors recognize bladder cancer sooner, prioritize patients who need testing, and potentially improve outcomes.
The study, "Early Detection of Bladder Cancer Using Advanced Feature Engineering and Swarm Intelligence Optimization on EHRs," was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering.
The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

articles.title: Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system
articles.text:
Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system
- Date:
  November 21, 2026
- Source:
  University of Virginia Health System
- Summary:
  Scientists have identified a gene that helps the brain’s immune cells contain harmful plaques linked to Alzheimer’s, potentially revealing a new way to fight the disease. When the gene malfunctioned in mice, toxic buildup accelerated and cognitive abilities declined, raising hopes that restoring its function could help protect the brain.
- Share:
A gene that helps the brain contain harmful protein buildup may play a crucial role in Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UVA Health have discovered that when this gene stops functioning properly, the brain's natural defenses become less effective, allowing toxic plaques to accumulate more rapidly. The findings could point toward new ways to detect, treat, or potentially prevent the disease.
The research, led by John Lukens, PhD, focused on a gene called CASS4, which previous studies had repeatedly linked to an increased risk of Alzheimer's. Until now, however, scientists knew little about what the gene actually does. The team discovered that CASS4 helps regulate microglia, specialized immune cells that act as the brain's cleanup and defense system. When the gene's activity was disrupted, these cells struggled to respond to harmful plaques. They also became much less effective at containing and compacting the toxic material, allowing the plaques to expand and spread more aggressively.
"These findings break new ground in our understanding of how this genetic risk factor contributes to Alzheimer's disease," said Lukens, director of UVA's Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases. "Our work further suggests that defective CASS4 activity may serve as an early-onset biomarker to detect Alzheimer's and that therapeutic strategies which boost its function may offer a much-needed approach to treat this devastating brain disease."
How the Brain's Cleanup System Protects Against Alzheimer's
More than 6 million Americans are living with Alzheimer's, a progressive disease that gradually damages memory and thinking abilities. As the condition advances, people can lose the ability to recognize even their closest family members, including their own children. Alzheimer's is the sixth-leading cause of death in the United States, according to the figures cited by the researchers.
Two major changes in the brain are associated with the disease. One is the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques, sticky deposits of protein that collect between nerve cells. The other is the formation of twisted tangles of a protein called tau. Both are hallmarks of Alzheimer's, but growing evidence suggests that the brain's immune system, particularly its microglia, also plays an important role in how the disease develops.
Microglia normally help protect the brain by responding to threats and managing harmful material. When amyloid-beta plaques appear, these immune cells can surround them with protective barriers and compress the deposits into smaller, more tightly packed structures. This containment process helps limit the damage the plaques can cause to surrounding brain tissue.
The UVA researchers found that CASS4 is important for maintaining this protective response. When the gene was disrupted in laboratory mice, microglia became less capable of controlling amyloid-beta plaques. As a result, the plaques accumulated more rapidly, nearby nerve cells called neurons suffered damage, and the animals experienced worsening cognitive function.
A Little-Known Alzheimer's Gene Reveals Its Role
"Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer's risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease. Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper," said Addie Walsh, UVA physiology graduate student and first author of the paper. "These are important findings because they give us new insight into how this understudied AD risk gene functions in the brain and suggest that CASS4 may normally help microglia respond to amyloid pathology."
The researchers also discovered that losing CASS4 set off a series of changes in the activity of other genes. These widespread effects could have implications beyond Alzheimer's, potentially helping explain biological processes involved in other neurodegenerative diseases, which progressively damage nerve cells.
One of the most significant findings was where CASS4 appears to exert its influence. Scientists had previously suspected that the gene contributed to Alzheimer's primarily through its effects on neurons, the cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain. Instead, the new research indicates that its main role is in the immune system.
That distinction could be important for developing future treatments. Rather than focusing exclusively on neurons or the proteins that accumulate in Alzheimer's, researchers may be able to strengthen the immune cells that help protect the brain from those deposits. The UVA team believes that increasing CASS4 activity or improving microglial function could eventually offer ways to slow or prevent the disease.
A Potential New Target for Alzheimer's Treatments
"We are now actively exploring potential roles for CASS4 in multiple other neurodegenerative disorders and developing novel strategies to therapeutically target it," said Lukens, of the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Virginia School of Medicine. "Many in the field initially presumed that CASS4 was likely functioning in neurons to influence Alzheimer's. Our findings shift this paradigm by proving that CASS4 predominantly acts through the immune system. This is particularly exciting, as it has only been in recent years that immune-targeting strategies have been considered for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, and this remains an untapped therapeutic avenue with tremendous potential."
The findings suggest that the brain's immune defenses may offer an important opportunity for future Alzheimer's therapies. They also raise the possibility that defective CASS4 activity could eventually serve as an early warning sign of the disease, potentially helping doctors identify people at risk before more serious symptoms develop.
However, these possibilities remain to be tested. The experiments showing increased plaque buildup, neuronal damage, and cognitive decline were conducted in mice. Further research will be needed to determine whether targeting CASS4 can produce similar protective effects in humans.
The work is part of a broader effort at UVA to translate laboratory discoveries into treatments for serious diseases. Lukens leads the Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases, which operates within UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute was created to accelerate the development of medicines and other therapies for complex medical conditions using advances from UVA's biomedical research programs.
Lukens is also a member of UVA's Center for Brain Immunology and Glia (BIG Center), which studies the roles of immune cells and other supporting cells in brain health and disease.
Walsh, meanwhile, is preparing to continue her research into the brain's immune system in a new position.
"I will be heading to Boston at the end of the year to start my postdoctoral research with the Neurodegeneration Team at the pharmaceutical company Novartis," she said. "I am looking forward to continuing to study microglia in neurodegeneration."
Alzheimer's Gene Discovery Published in Scientific Journal
The research was published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine. The authors are Adeline E. Walsh, Benjamin A. Davis, Joshua D. Samuels, William A. Mills III, Jessica M. Thanos, Alexis M. Johnson, Katelyn A. Moore, Michael A. Puchalski, Eric J. Steacy, Benjamin W. Wendell, Amélie Daugherty-Lopès, Adrian A. Shimpi, Ukpong B. Eyo and Lukens. The researchers reported having no financial interest in the work.
Among the contributors is Davis, a fourth-year biology student at UVA, who says participating in scientific research has helped shape his approach to problem-solving and his plans for a career in medicine.
"I think that undergraduate research develops a kind of critical thinking that is difficult to cultivate inside a classroom," he said. "My experience with research has taught me to approach questions systematically and never assume there will be a clear answer. As I prepare to apply to medical school, I know these experiences will shape how I approach clinical care and the broader field of science."
Funding came from the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging through grants R01AG071996, R01AG087406, RF1AG078684 and R01AG086344. Additional support was provided by the Cure Alzheimer's Fund, the Owens Family Foundation, the Harrison Family Foundation, the Rick Sharp Foundation, and the Steven A. Newman AD Award.
